content.text: Lesson 3 Overview

Renewable energy is often linked to its ability to generate electricity with minimal greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. This is a crucial factor in the global effort to mitigate climate change. As the climate crisis intensifies, renewable energy’s role in reducing emissions becomes even more vital. It plays a key part in achieving climate targets. This was highlighted at COP28, where countries agreed to triple global renewable energy capacity by 2030. This commitment aligns with the actions needed to meet global climate goals.

content.intro: M6: The Climate Change-Energy Nexus | Chapter 1 | Lesson 1 | Part 2
content.title: A: Renewable Energy Trade-offs

content.text: This section builds on Module 3 by exploring the specific impacts of renewable energy technologies on ecosystems and strategies to mitigate them. While renewables are essential for reducing emissions, their development can disrupt habitats and biodiversity if not carefully managed. Here, we examine these challenges in greater detail and explore solutions such as sustainable siting, ecological safeguards, and integrated approaches to ensure a truly sustainable energy transition.
1: Land Use Conflicts

The land requirements for different energy generation methods vary significantly, especially when considering their entire life cycle. Life-cycle land use assessments account not only for the physical footprint of the energy plant itself but also for the land required for activities like mining materials for construction, sourcing fuel inputs, decommissioning, and managing waste. The construction of renewable energy facilities, such as solar farms and wind turbines, requires significantly more land to produce the same amount of electricity as a coal-fired power plant. This can lead to habitat fragmentation and displacement of wildlife.

Ground mounted solar installations tend to have relatively high land use, although this varies based on location and the configuration of the solar panels. For instance, utility-scale solar farms, unlike rooftop solar panels, can disrupt local ecosystems by occupying large tracts of land, altering habitats, and driving species away from their natural environments. While it is true that rooftop solar installations use significantly less land, as they utilize existing structures, their land use is not zero, as mining materials for solar panel production still require land resources.

A study analyzing solar energy land use in regions like the European Union, India, and South Korea highlight a key concern: as solar energy becomes a larger share of a region's electricity mix, associated land-use changes and emissions also grow. Solar expansion often takes place on land currently used for agriculture or forestry. This displacement can push agricultural or forestry activities to other areas, often involving unused arable land, resulting in natural land cover losses. These changes disturb local ecosystems and release carbon stored in soils and vegetation, offsetting some of the environmental benefits of solar energy.

Another study on a 96 MW solar installation in South Africa found a significant decline in bird species diversity and density. The replacement of the natural savanna with solar panels and managed grasslands disrupted habitats, reducing nesting and foraging opportunities for local bird populations. These land-use challenges also intersect with social considerations, particularly in the context of achieving a just energy transition 💬️ (previously discussed in Module 3). Large-scale projects can have varied impacts on local communities, raising concerns about equitable access to opportunities and minimizing risks for those most affected by renewable energy expansion.
2: Energy Infrastructure and Biodiversity Risks

The infrastructure required for renewable energy projects can also impact local ecosystems and livelihoods. Wind farms can pose threats to birds and bats due to collisions with turbine blades, while hydroelectric projects can disrupt aquatic habitats and alter water flow patterns. Nevertheless, research and conservation efforts are underway to identify best practices for developing energy infrastructure in a way that minimizes damage to biodiversity and ecosystem services.

Mineral Intensity of the Energy Transition
The transition requires vast quantities of “critical energy transition minerals” (CETMs), including lithium, cobalt, nickel, copper, and rare earth elements. An onshore wind plant requires nine times more mineral inputs than a gas-fired plant of the same capacity, and an electric vehicle uses six times more minerals than a conventional car.
Development and Social Challenges for Producer Nations
This mineral intensity creates a development dilemma for producer nations. While demand for these minerals is projected to grow fivefold by 2030, the extraction process is linked to severe environmental degradation, including soil erosion, water contamination, and ecosystem damage. Furthermore, approximately 54% of these minerals are located on or near Indigenous and local community lands. Disputes over land rights and environmental damage have fueled more than 36,000 mining-related conflict events globally between 2015 and 2022. In the Salar de Atacama, Chile, lithium and copper extraction consumes over 65% of the local water supply, worsening drought conditions and threatening the livelihoods of pastoral communities.
3: Mining for Renewable Resources

Environmental Impacts of Mining for Renewable Energy
The transition to renewable energy necessitates increased mining activities for essential materials like lithium, cobalt, and rare earth elements. Mining operations often result in severe environmental degradation, including soil erosion, water pollution, and destruction of habitats. In fact, many reserves of critical minerals 💬️ for renewable power infrastructure coincide with areas of high biodiversity value. In regions where these minerals are extracted, such as the Atacama Desert in Chile, mining activities have been attributed to being one of the major stressors to local environmental degradation. Similarly, in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), home to one of the world’s largest rainforests, cobalt mining has raised major environmental and human rights concerns, including deforestation, water contamination, and child labor.
Deep sea mining is also being explored to meet mineral demand, targeting resources on the ocean floor. However, it poses serious risks to marine ecosystems, including habitat destruction and loss of biodiversity, raising concerns about its environmental impact.
4: Managing the Full Lifecycle of Renewable Energy Infrastructure

The decommissioning of renewable energy infrastructure is an often-overlooked challenge that has long-term implications for energy systems and sustainability. Wind turbines, solar panels, and hydropower facilities all have finite lifespans; typically 20-30 years for solar panels and wind turbines, and up to 100 years for hydropower plants. For offshore wind farms, decommissioning involves dismantling turbines, removing subsea structures, and managing waste materials. Without proper planning, this process could disrupt marine ecosystems and create large quantities of waste. Similarly, solar panel disposal raises concerns about e-waste and the recycling of rare materials like silicon, silver, and cadmium. Hydropower plants, especially older ones, may require retrofitting or removal, which can significantly impact water systems and local ecosystems. A lack of decommissioning strategies could lead to stranded assets and increased environmental impacts.

content.title: A: Addressing Renewable Energy Trade-offs

content.text: 1: Site Selection

Prioritizing the development of renewable energy projects on degraded or previously disturbed lands rather than pristine ecosystems can help minimize habitat destruction. Utilizing brownfield sites for solar installations is one approach that reduces land-use conflicts.

content.title: Prioritize Degraded Lands
content.body: Focusing on the development of renewable energy projects on degraded or previously disturbed lands rather than pristine ecosystems is crucial. This strategy minimizes habitat destruction and helps preserve biodiversity. For instance, utilizing rooftops or brownfield sites for solar installations can significantly reduce land-use conflicts and environmental degradation.

content.title: Avoid High-Conflict Areas
content.body: Siting policies should exclude high-yield cropland and other ecologically sensitive areas to limit land competition and adverse impacts. Instead, regions such as deserts or dry scrublands, which are less suitable for agriculture and human activities, should be prioritized for solar energy installations.

content.title: Incorporate Local Ecological Considerations
content.body: Effective spatial planning that includes ecosystem and wildlife sensitivity mapping is essential. Identifying "Renewables Acceleration Areas" through rigorous assessments can help balance renewable energy development with ecological preservation. This involves considering local community needs and potential conflicts to ensure sustainable project siting.

content.text: 2: Integrated Planning

Incorporating biodiversity considerations into energy planning processes is essential. This includes assessing the potential ecological impacts of proposed projects and implementing measures to protect sensitive habitats.

content.title: Conduct Comprehensive Environmental Assessments
content.body: Before initiating any renewable energy project, it is crucial to conduct thorough environmental impact assessments (EIAs). These assessments should evaluate potential ecological impacts, including effects on local wildlife, plant species, and overall ecosystem health.

content.title: Utilize Geospatial Analysis
content.body: Employing geospatial tools and technologies can help in mapping sensitive habitats and biodiversity hotspots. This information can guide site selection and project design, ensuring that developments avoid critical areas and minimize disruptions to local ecosystems.

content.title: Implement Mitigation Strategies
content.body: For projects that may impact sensitive habitats, it is important to develop and implement mitigation strategies. These could include habitat restoration efforts, creating wildlife corridors, or establishing conservation easements to protect affected areas.

content.title: Engage Stakeholders
content.body: Involving local communities, conservation organizations, and other stakeholders in the planning process is vital. Their insights can provide valuable perspectives on biodiversity concerns and help identify areas of ecological significance that may not be readily apparent through standard assessments.

content.text:
Innovative practices are emerging to address these land-use conflicts. Agrivoltaics, for example, combines solar energy 💬️ production with agricultural activities, allowing crops to be grown beneath or between solar panels.
Agrivoltaic systems are being implemented in Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda, where the shade provided by solar panels helps shield crops from extreme heat and minimizes water evaporation from both plants and soil. This approach has led to improved yields and healthier crops, including cabbage, eggplant, lettuce, and maize.
Additionally, pollinator-friendly solar farms are gaining traction. These involve planting wildflowers and native vegetation under and around solar panels to support pollinators, improve soil quality, and preserve the land for potential future agricultural use. Such solutions help balance the expansion of solar energy with environmental conservation and sustainable land management.
3: Green Production Inputs and Processes

Incorporating green production and responsible practices into renewable energy supply chains is essential. This involves sourcing low-carbon materials and adopting sustainable manufacturing techniques to minimize emissions and waste.

content.title: Implement Cradle-to-Cradle Design
content.body:
Adopting a cradle-to-cradle* approach in manufacturing focuses on designing products that can be fully reclaimed or recycled at the end of their life cycle. This minimizes waste and promotes the use of materials that can be continuously re-purposed, thereby reducing the demand for new raw materials.

*Cradle to cradle can be defined as the design and production of products of all types in such a way that at the end of their life, they can be truly recycled (upcycled), imitating nature’s cycle with everything either recycled or returned to the earth, directly or indirectly through food, as a completely safe, nontoxic, and biodegradable nutrient.

content.title: Switch to Renewable Energy Sources & Enhance Energy Efficiency
content.body: Powering manufacturing processes with renewable energy, such as solar, wind, or geothermal, can significantly reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Moreover, upgrading to smart lighting systems, optimizing heating and cooling systems, and using advanced manufacturing techniques that minimize energy consumption can help improve energy efficiency.

content.title: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle
content.body: Establishing robust recycling programs and initiatives to reduce waste is crucial in green manufacturing. Companies should conduct waste audits to identify recyclable materials and implement practices that minimize waste generation during production.

content.title: Focus on Pollution Reduction
content.body: Adopting processes that limit the release of pollutants into the environment is essential. This can involve using non-toxic materials and cleaner production techniques that reduce harmful emissions and improve overall environmental performance.

content.text: Restoration Efforts
Alongside energy development, efforts should be made to restore degraded ecosystems. Reforestation initiatives can help recover lost habitats and enhance carbon sequestration capabilities.
Capacity Building and Technical Expertise

content.title: Training Programs
content.body: Developing a skilled workforce through targeted training initiatives can help address the technical expertise gap necessary for deploying and maintaining renewable technologies effectively.

content.title: Public-Private Partnerships
content.body: Collaborations between governments, private sector entities, and non-profit organizations can facilitate knowledge transfer and resource sharing, enhancing local capabilities in renewable technology implementation.

content.text: Community Engagement and Awareness

content.title: Local Involvement
content.body: Engaging communities in the planning and execution of renewable projects ensures that solutions are tailored to local needs, enhancing acceptance and sustainability.

content.title: Awareness Campaigns
content.body: Educating communities about the benefits and the associated risks of renewable energy can drive demand and support for clean energy initiatives, overcoming resistance based on a lack of information.

content.title: Case Study: Georgia
content.subtitle: Renewable Energy Practices For Sustainable Forest Management And Enhanced Community Resilience

content.text:
In the remote highlands of Georgia, survival often meant cutting down the very forests that shielded communities from the harsh effects of climate extremes. Over 95% of rural households relied on firewood for heating and cooking, resulting in nearby woodlands being rapidly depleted as fuel reserves (CENN, 2016, p. 2). This heavy reliance on biomass 💬️ drove carbon emissions higher, contributed to deforestation, and degraded local ecosystems, accelerating erosion, floods, and water scarcity. Women bore the brunt of this burden, spending hours gathering fuelwood while children were exposed to harmful indoor air pollution. Georgia’s aging energy infrastructure is under-resourced and poorly integrated with climate resilience planning, lagging behind EU benchmarks and reinforcing an unsustainable cycle of poverty and environmental decline.

To break this cycle, Georgia did not simply import clean technologies; it redefined how energy, forests, and people could co-exist. Through a joint UNDP–GEF initiative, decentralized renewable energy solutions, including solar water heaters, biogas units, and efficient stoves, were distributed across forest-edge villages. What set this approach apart was its integration into Community-Based Forest Management Plans. These were not just equipment handouts; they were climate solutions embedded into local governance structures. Training centers were established to ensure maintenance and build skills, while implementation was increasingly led by women, reflecting a growing commitment to gender-responsive climate action. This participatory model, as seen in the Machakhela Forest Management Initiative (UNDP Georgia), shifted energy from being a driver of degradation to a pillar of forest protection.

The systems themselves were designed for local needs:

Solar thermal heaters reduced the wood used for water heating
Biogas units reuse livestock waste to cook food
Efficient stoves cut household firewood use in half

According to the official UNDP project document for the Machakhela renewable energy initiative (UNDP Georgia, 2023), the intervention was designed to achieve the following within two years:
30% reduction in household firewood use (UNDP Georgia, 2023)
87 tons of CO₂ emissions avoided annually (UNDP Georgia, 2023)
1,350 beneficiaries, including at least 40% from women-led households (UNDP Georgia, 2023)
210 hectares of forest area are protected annually (UNDP, 2020)
The model is being scaled to other protected areas in Georgia, including Kakheti. (UNDP, 2020)

However, the change took time and effort. Georgia’s mountainous terrain created logistical challenges, including delays in spare part delivery, which left some systems inoperable. Many residents were also hesitant to switch from traditional wood fires. These issues were addressed through community involvement and shared decision-making. Forest-user groups took responsibility for managing energy system distribution, maintenance, and oversight. This inclusive approach helped build trust and ensured long-term adoption.

content.text:
Georgia’s experience shows how community-centered energy solutions can support both climate goals and forest conservation. By aligning renewable energy with local priorities, the project reduced environmental damage and empowered residents, especially women, to lead implementation. Instead of relying on large grid infrastructure, the focus was on practical, decentralized systems that directly improved daily life in rural areas.
Replicability depends on three main ingredients:
Acknowledging the emissions and land-use cost of traditional fuels
Embedding renewable energy into local governance frameworks
Investing in community infrastructure and long-term trust (CENN, 2022)

As Georgia scales this model through its National Forest Program, it proves that climate resilience does not have to be distant, technical, or abstract. It can start in a stove, a solar tank, or a forest edge and spread from there.

takeaways.title: Diverse Renewable Technologies are Key to Emission Reductions.
takeaways.description: Solar, wind, hydropower, geothermal, and hydrogen are playing a crucial role in reducing greenhouse gas emissions and accelerating the global energy transition. Each technology has unique advantages, such as solar PV’s affordability, wind energy’s scalability, hydropower’s grid stability, geothermal’s reliability, and hydrogen’s potential for hard-to-abate sectors.

takeaways.title: Implementation Challenges Must Be Addressed.
takeaways.description: While renewable energy technologies offer significant benefits, their implementation faces challenges, including high initial investment costs, grid integration issues, financing constraints, and infrastructure limitations, particularly in developing countries.

takeaways.title: Strategic Approaches are Essential for Scaling Renewable Energy.
takeaways.description: Policy incentives, innovative financing (e.g., blended finance and concessional loans), infrastructure development (grid modernization and energy storage), capacity building, and community engagement are key strategies for scaling up renewable energy deployment, ensuring equitable access, and supporting a just energy transition.
